`sim.fit()` always returns values. Whether to trust them is a separate question, with several parts: does the model match the data, did the search find the best values, are the values determined by the data, and would the fitted model predict data it hasn't seen? This page goes through the checks, in the order worth making them. It assumes the basics of [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd).

The examples use a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune. The data are a year of weekly reported cases, made from the model with a latent period of 10 days (an SEIR model), `beta = 1.9`, and half of all cases reported:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

def make_seir():
    """ Measles with a latent period: infected (E), then infectious (I) about 10 days later """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    onset  = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    cases  = ss.outcome(report*onset)
    return ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
truth = ss.Sim(make_seir(), pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')
```

## Does the model match the data?

Start by looking. A fit can converge perfectly and still be wrong, if the model can't produce the pattern in the data. Here the data are fitted with a model that leaves out the latent period, an SIR model:

```{python}
def make_sir():
    """ Measles without a latent period: infectious as soon as infected """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    cases     = ss.outcome(report*infection)
    return ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

sir_fit = ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars).fit()
```

The search converged, but the share reported ended at its upper bound of 1 (with an `AtBound` warning). `fit.plot(residuals=True)` shows why: the model's weekly cases before and after fitting against the data, and below them the difference between the data and the fitted model (the residuals), on the data's own weeks, as the fit compares them:

```{python}
sir_fit.plot(residuals=True)
```

Without a latent period, an epidemic with the same R0 grows much faster, so the SIR model can't be both as late and as large as the data: it peaks too early and too low, even with every case reported. The residuals have a pattern: too many cases in the model early on, then too few through the peak. Residuals that wander above and below zero at random, as for the right model below, are what a good fit looks like:

```{python}
seir_fit = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars).fit(verbose=False)
seir_fit.plot(residuals=True)
```

A pattern in the residuals points to the structure of the model, or to how the data were defined, not to the fitting: no search will fix it. Some common patterns, and what to look at first:

| Pattern | Things to examine |
|---|---|
| The peak consistently too early or too late | The initial infections and when they are introduced; the latent period; reporting delays |
| The right shape but the wrong size | The population size; the share reported; whether the data count events (a flow) or people at a time (a stock) |
| A best value at a bound | The bounds; a missing process that the parameter is making up for; weak identification |
| Different starts giving different answers | Several optima, too short a search, a noisy objective |
| A good fit but an unstable projection | Parameters the data can't tell apart; a change in the epidemic the model doesn't have |

Before blaming the model, check that like is compared with like: incidence with case counts over the same interval, prevalence with a survey at a time, hospital admissions with admissions rather than beds occupied, and dates aligned (Starsim dates a count by the start of its period, so a week starting on a Monday is dated by that Monday, and data dated by the end of each week needs moving back a week). The fit's measure (`fit.objective`) helps compare fits to the same data, here 0.38 for the SIR model against 0.10 for the SEIR model, but the plot shows *where* a model fails.

## Did the search converge?

Every fit says whether it converged, and how it decided, in `fit.converged` and `fit.why`, which are also printed:

```{python}
print(seir_fit.converged)
print(seir_fit.why)
```

What "converged" means depends on the method: for an optimizer, that searches from different starts end at the same value, or that the best score has stopped improving; for a sampler, that its chains agree. The rule of every method, and what to do if it fails, is in the [appendix](#appendix-when-each-method-has-converged).

A fit that has not converged is not necessarily wrong, but it can't be trusted until it has been run longer, or until the reason it didn't is understood.

## Is a best value at a bound?

A best value at the edge of its bounds triggers an `AtBound` warning, as for the SIR model above. It means one of three things:

- The true value is beyond the bound: widen it, if larger (or smaller) values are plausible.
- The data don't determine the parameter, so nothing stops it drifting to the edge (see [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd)).
- The model is missing something, and the parameter is being pushed to the edge to make up for it, as the reporting share was above. Widening its bounds to allow more than 100% of cases to be reported would make the fit better and the model worse.

## Does the fit give the same answer again?

A stochastic model is fitted to noisy scores, so a second fit, with another `rand_seed=`, shows how much the answer depends on chance. Here the model is run as a chain binomial (a stochastic compartmental model), and fitted twice:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

stochastic = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
rows = []
for seed in [1, 2]:
    fit = stochastic.fit(rand_seed=seed, verbose=False, method=ss.fit.method('optuna', n_trials=100))
    rows.append(dict(rand_seed=seed, beta=fit.pars.beta, report=fit.pars.report, converged=fit.converged))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
```

The two fits differ, by more in the share reported than in β (against true values of 1.9 and 0.5), and the `converged` column says whether each search had stopped improving by its end. Even a fit that says it has converged has only stopped improving; that doesn't make the answer precise. The noise in the scores is large compared with the difference that `report` makes to them. More trials, or more runs for each trial (`n_runs=`, 4 by default for a stochastic compartmental model), reduce this; so does a likelihood, which weighs the data by how much they vary, and with which Optuna scores each trial by a particle filter's estimate of the likelihood rather than by runs. The fit also reruns its best values with the same seeds as the search, and warns when they then score worse than the starting values: the best trial may have been a lucky run.

For a stochastic model, also check the fit against many runs, not one: `ss.parallel(fit.sim, n_runs=20)`, as in [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd#a-stochastic-model). Expect the data to fall outside the range of the runs more often than the interval suggests: the runs leave out the noise in how the data were observed (the likelihood's), and runs at one set of values leave out the uncertainty in the parameters.

## Does the time step matter?

A model run as agents or as a chain binomial takes whole steps, and when its rates are fast compared with the step, the step changes the results (see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#the-length-of-a-step)), and so the fitted values: a fit with daily steps can find a higher β to make up for the delay the steps add. `fit.sim.check_dt()` reruns the fitted sim with half the step and shows how much each result changes; if they change by more than the mismatch of the fit, fit again with the smaller step.

## Can the data tell the parameters apart?

Starsim notes when two parameters can't be told apart: when they appear in the model only multiplied together, or (for a posterior) when they are almost perfectly correlated. Even without a note, check that the fit can recover known values from data made by the model itself, as this page's examples do. [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd) covers this in detail.

## Is the posterior reliable?

For a posterior by NUTS or particle MCMC (`method='nuts'` or `'pmcmc'`), `fit.summarize()` prints a table with the posterior's median and 95% interval for each parameter, and two checks for each (ABC-SMC's has the effective sample size only, and its convergence is not assessed; see the [appendix](#appendix-when-each-method-has-converged)):

- **R-hat** (`rhat`): compares the spread within each chain with the spread between chains. Near 1 means the chains have found the same distribution; above 1.01, they disagree, and the posterior is not yet reliable.
- **Effective sample size** (`ess`): how many independent draws the correlated draws are worth. A few hundred is enough for a median and a 95% interval.

NUTS also counts **divergent** draws (`fit.diagnostics.divergences`), where the sampler's path went wrong in a region of sharp curvature; even a few mean the posterior may be missing a region. If any of these checks fail, the fit warns (`ss.errors.NotConverged`). More warm-up (`warmup=`) sometimes fixes it, but a common cause is a ridge, where the data determine only a combination of parameters: then fix one, or get more data. An example of a posterior with a ridge is in [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd).

## Looking at the search

For a fit by Optuna, `fit.study` is Optuna's own record of the search, which its plots take: how the best score improved over the trials (has it leveled off?), which parameters mattered most to the score, and the score over each pair of parameters (a long diagonal valley is a ridge that the data can't resolve). These need Plotly:

```python
import optuna
optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_contour(fit.study, params=['beta', 'report'])
```

For any method, `fit.to_df()` has every evaluation, with the values tried and the objective at each, for plots of your own; [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd#which-combinations-the-data-determine) has one.

## Does the model predict?

A model with more parameters usually fits better, without necessarily being better. A fairer test is how well a model fitted to the start of the data predicts the rest. `ss.fit.compare_models()` fits each model to the data before a cut, runs it forward, and scores it on the part held out. By default the last 25% of each series is held out, but here that would be the decline after the August peak, which is easy to predict once the peak has been fitted. The question a modeler usually faces is whether a model fitted to the rise of an outbreak predicts its peak, so `holdout=` gives a date instead: two months, and then one month, before the peak:

```{python}
models = {'SIR': ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars), 'SEIR': ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars)}
for cut in ['2025-06-01', '2025-07-01']:
    comparison = ss.fit.compare_models(models, method='nelder-mead', holdout=cut, verbose=False)
    comparison.summarize()
```

With data to the start of July, the SEIR model predicts the rest of the outbreak much better than the SIR model. With data only to the start of June, both predict it badly: two months before the peak, the rise of the outbreak says too little about how high it will go for either model, the right one included. A good fit to the data so far is not a good prediction. A stochastic model is scored over many runs at its best values (`n_runs=`, 100 by default), by the log of the mean of their likelihoods (or by their mean loss). The runs start at the beginning and are not conditioned on the data fitted to, so the score is harsher on a stochastic model than on an ODE, and it is at the best values only, not over a posterior. `folds=` repeats the comparison over several cut points, which shows whether the difference is larger than the spread from one cut point to another; `comparison.plot()` shows each model's fit and prediction against the data (here, for the last cut). Both models were fitted to data made by the SEIR model, so the right one is known here; with real data, every model is wrong to some extent, and this comparison says which predicts better.

## A checklist

| Check | How | A problem looks like |
|---|---|---|
| The model matches the data | Plot the model against the data, on the data's own periods, and the residuals (`fit.plot(residuals=True)`) | A pattern in the residuals; a parameter pushed to a bound |
| The search converged | `fit.converged`, `fit.why` | "Not converged", with the reason |
| No value is at a bound | The `AtBound` warning | A best value at the edge |
| The answer is stable | Fit again with another `rand_seed=` (stochastic) or from other starting points (`scan=`) | Different values each time |
| The parameters are identifiable | A note that they can't be told apart; recover known values | A ridge, or values that move together |
| The posterior is reliable | `rhat`, `ess`, divergences | R-hat above 1.01, few effective draws, any divergences |
| The model predicts | `ss.fit.compare_models()` | A model that fits well but predicts badly |
| The fit is plausible | Compare the values with what is known from elsewhere | A reporting share above 1, an infectious period of months |

The last check matters most, and no software can make it: a fit only finds the values that make this model match these data. Whether those values, and the model, make sense for the disease and the setting is a judgment for the modeler.

When reporting a fit, say enough for someone else to repeat it and judge it: what each data series is and how it was matched to the model (flow or stock, over what periods); the measure of fit or the likelihood; the parameters fitted, with their bounds and priors, and those held fixed and why; the method, its settings, and the seed; the diagnostics above; and the versions of Starsim and of the data.

## Further reading

- [Stan: Posterior predictive checks](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/posterior-predictive-checks.html): checking a fitted model against data it should reproduce
- [Optuna: Visualization](https://optuna.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/visualization/index.html): the plots of a search that `fit.study` takes
- [ArviZ](https://python.arviz.org/en/stable/): R-hat, effective sample size, and plots for checking a posterior
- [pomp: Getting started](https://kingaa.github.io/pomp/vignettes/getting_started.html): diagnostics of fits of stochastic models, including iterated filtering

## Appendix: when each method has converged

The rule by which each method sets `fit.converged` (and says why in `fit.why`), and what to try if it hasn't:

| Method | Converged when | If not |
|---|---|---|
| SciPy optimizers (`'nelder-mead'`, `'powell'`, `'l-bfgs-b'`, `'slsqp'`) | The two best searches, from the best few points of a scan that are apart, end at the same value (with a single search, SciPy's own stopping rule) | More starting points (`scan=`) or searches (`restarts=`), or more iterations (`maxiter=`); a sign of several local optima, or a ridge |
| Optuna (`'optuna'`) | The best score improved by less than 1% over the last quarter of the trials, and the best trial is not one of the first 10 (which are random) or the starting values | More trials (`n_trials=`) |
| Iterated filtering (`'if2'`) | Chains from different starts end within 2 of the best log-likelihood | More passes (`iterations=`) or particles (`particles=`); better bounds, if a chain has wandered off where the outbreak dies out |
| NUTS (`'nuts'`) | The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01) and no draws diverged | More warm-up (`warmup=`) and draws; check identifiability |
| Particle MCMC (`'pmcmc'`) | The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01) | More draws and warm-up; more particles, if the acceptance is low |
| ABC-SMC (`'abc-smc'`) | Not assessed (`fit.converged` is None): its result approximates the posterior, as closely as the final tolerance allows, and no rule says when that is close enough. `fit.why` and `fit.diagnostics` give the final tolerance, the share of the last generation's proposals accepted, and the number of generations | More generations (`generations=`) for a smaller tolerance, or more samples (`samples=`); with a likelihood, `'pmcmc'` |
| A list of methods | Its last stage converged; a stage that doesn't stops the list, with a warning, and its fit (or the last that converged) is returned | Make that stage converge, by its own rule |

A best fit of a stochastic model that converged is also marked as not converged if, rerun with the same seeds, its best values score worse than the starting values: the best trial may have been a lucky run.

## Appendix: the warnings and notes a fit gives

Each message a fit can print, what it means, and what to do. Warnings are Python warnings (some of a class of their own, which `warnings.filterwarnings()` can select); notes are printed, and are silenced with `verbose=False`.

| Message | Kind | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| The best-fit value is at one of its bounds | Warning, `ss.errors.AtBound` | The best value may lie beyond the bound, or the data don't determine the parameter, or it is making up for something missing | [Above](#is-a-best-value-at-a-bound): widen the bounds only if larger (or smaller) values are plausible |
| The profile stays within the threshold up to a bound | Warning, `ss.errors.AtBound` | A profile likelihood's interval may extend beyond the bounds | Wider bounds, or more values |
| Not converged, with the reason | Printed, and in `fit.why` | The method's own rule (above) was not met | As in the table above |
| The chains disagree (R-hat above 1.01), or draws diverged | Warning, `ss.errors.NotConverged` | A posterior that is not yet reliable | More warm-up; check identifiability ([above](#is-the-posterior-reliable)) |
| A stage did not converge, so the stages after it were not run | Warning | A list of methods stopped early | Make that stage converge (e.g. more trials) |
| Rerun with the same seeds, the best values score worse than the initial values | Printed, and in `fit.why` | In a stochastic fit, the best trial may have been a lucky run | More trials (`n_trials=`), or more runs or particles per trial (`n_runs=`, `particles=`) |
| Two parameters appear in the model only multiplied together (or one divided by the other) | Note | Structurally unidentifiable: the data determine only their product | Fit one and fix the other ([Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd)) |
| Two parameters are almost perfectly correlated in the posterior (r above 0.95), or change the fitted results in almost the same way | Note | Practically unidentifiable from these data | More data, or data of another kind, or fix one |
| The scan tries fewer than 10 points for each parameter | Note | With more than 10 parameters, the scan is capped at 100 points | `scan=` to change it |
| The R-hat and effective sample size need JAX | Note | Without BlackJAX, they are NaN, so a posterior can't be checked | `pip install "starsim[jax]"` |
| The fit would take the gradients (or the posterior) with Python in the loop | Error, `ss.CapabilityError` | A method with gradients was asked for, but something in the model or the likelihood can't be run in JAX (e.g. a likelihood given as a function, or an initial value or share that is not linear in the fitted parameters), so they would be much slower (the default method falls back to Nelder-Mead by itself) | A method without gradients (e.g. `method='nelder-mead'`, or no `method=`), or `require_jax=False` to accept the slower way |
| A data column matches no result | Note when the sim is initialized, and an error when it is fitted | A typo in a header, or a result that doesn't exist | Rename the column (`ss.SimData(aliases=...)`) |
